turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through, love. We'll get your obs done before the doctor. Check-up, is it?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, well, my wife booked it. She reckons I've been putting it off, and I'm a bit wound up. Does this usually take long?
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Not too long if the computer behaves. Arm out for me, sleeve up.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): That cuff's pinching. Is it meant to squeeze like that? Sorry, I hate these.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): That's just the machine. Blood pressure is one forty-eight over eighty-six. Pulse is seventy-eight, and your oxygen sat is ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): One forty-eight. Is that high? Should I be panicking? I googled it last night and that was a mistake.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): I wouldn't panic. Doctor will talk you through it. Any allergies?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm allergic to. Not that I know of — no, nothing.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Ta. Have a seat, he'll be in. He's wrestling with the screen again.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right, sorry. This thing's frozen twice already. Can you remind me what we're doing today? The referral bit is blank.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): It's just a check-up. I'm Graham Holt. Haven't been in for, oh, a fair while.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Graham Holt, yep, got you. How old are you? The date of birth's tiny on here.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm sixty-three. Sixty-four in March. Is the date wrong on your screen?
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): No, it's there, I just can't read it. Any worries, or are we doing the whole once-over?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly the once-over. I have been a bit puffed walking the dog, though. My brother had a heart thing and it plays on my mind. Is being puffed serious?
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, a window popped up over your notes. Puffed walking the dog — say that again for me?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): When I walk him fast, or up that hill by the oval, I get short of breath. Not every time. It's been the last month or so, and if I slow down I'm alright.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I wouldn't call it pain.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. Medicines. Are you still on a blood pressure tablet?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): The little white one, yeah, for the blood pressure. Every morning, with breakfast. I don't miss that one.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): What's the name? I've got two antihypertensives in the old list and the screen won't tell me which you stopped.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the chemist bottle says Coversyl, five milligrams. I've been on it for years. That's the one, isn't it? I didn't stop anything.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Coversyl five milligrams in the morning, we'll keep that as current. What about aspirin?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I take a Cartia, on and off, when I remember. Maybe three or four times a week. Should I be on it every day? I read something about bleeding and now I'm second-guessing it.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll sort the aspirin in a minute. Any diabetes, asthma, operations?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No operations, and no diabetes. Dad had blood pressure, that's the family stuff really. I don't smoke, gave that up years ago. Couple of beers on the weekend, that's it.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hang on, it scrolled. You gave up smoking — how long ago? Say it again.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I said years. Ten years, easy — actually more like twelve. Yeah, about twelve years. Sorry, I'm all over the shop today.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're fine. Let me have a listen to your chest. Big breath in.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear. Heart sounds are fine, no murmurs. Nurse has you at one forty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight, sats ninety-eight.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): If the heart sounds are fine, does that mean I'm in the clear? Only, going up the stairs at home there's this tight feeling across the chest. I'm worried I should've said.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tight feeling. You told me no chest pain before. Run that past me again, the printer just kicked off and I missed the first bit.

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I said it wasn't pain. It's a tightness, like a band across my chest, when I climb the stairs or if I'm walking fast. It comes on after a flight of stairs, and if I stop it settles in a minute or two. Been a few weeks — is that a heart attack waiting to happen?

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I can't tell you it's a heart attack from a listen and a chat. It could be angina, that exertional tightness, but that's a working idea, not a diagnosis. We'll need an ECG and some bloods.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Today? Does the ECG hurt? And will I have to take my shirt off in front of everyone?

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): ECG doesn't hurt, stickers on the chest, shirt off in the side room. I'll order it now, plus bloods for cholesterol, sugar, kidney function, and a troponin because of the tightness.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Troponin, that's the heart-attack blood test, yeah? If it's up, does that mean I've already had one? I need you to say it plainly.

[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): It means the heart muscle may have been under strain, and if it's raised we deal with it today. I'm also going to start you on a GTN spray, under the tongue, if that tightness comes on and doesn't ease when you rest.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): A spray, I've never had one of those. How many squirts, and am I taking the Cartia every day or not? I keep going around in circles, sorry.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): One spray under the tongue, and if it's not easing after five minutes, a second spray. If it's still there after that, ring an ambulance, don't drive. And yes, take the Cartia every day from now, one tablet in the morning, not just when you remember.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. What if it happens in the middle of the night? Can I still walk the dog, or is that me being stupid?

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Walk him, just don't push into the tightness. Stop, rest, and use the spray if it isn't settling, same rule at night. If you get sweaty, or the pain goes into the arm or the jaw, or you feel dizzy with it, that's straight to emergency.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't had sweating. No pain in the jaw. I don't think I've been dizzy, and I'll try not to google it again.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. Nurse will do the ECG before you go, and the bloods. Come back and see me in a week for the results, regardless.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): A week. What if the ECG is crook today, do I just sit at home worrying? I know I ask too many questions.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): If today's ECG or the troponin looks worrying, we won't wait, we'll sort it today. Otherwise it's one week.
[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): Did you want me? I was restocking the trolley.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. ECG now, and the bloods I mentioned — lipids, glucose, EUC, troponin.
[SEG0050] person_1 (NURSE): Side room's free. I'll set the ECG up.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Do the results come through on my phone, or do I have to ring? And who rings me if it's bad?
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): They come back onto the file, so don't sit by the phone. If something's urgent we'll contact you. Otherwise it's the appointment in a week.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. And the Coversyl, I keep taking the little white one the same? I don't want to muck that up.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Same dose, five milligrams every morning. Don't stop it.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks. I feel a bit silly, I nearly talked myself out of mentioning the tight feeling.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): You were right to say it. Come through when you're ready and we'll get that ECG done.

Continue Coversyl 5 mg every morning and do not stop it

spec.situation: Man or woman 50-70 who comes 'for a check-up' and only slowly admits a tight feeling in the chest when climbing stairs or walking fast; first denies chest pain, later describes the tightness. Takes a BP tablet and aspirin on and off. Doctor orders ECG and bloods.
features: colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Bloods planned, but transcript says cholesterol/sugar/kidney function, not specifically lipids/glucose/EUC.
bad.text: Blood tests for lipids, glucose, EUC and troponin (type=laboratory, status=planned, requested_by=doctor, indication=exertional chest tightness)

bad.reason: Doctor orders bloods, but names cholesterol/sugar/kidney function rather than lipids/glucose/EUC explicitly.
bad.text: Order blood tests for lipids, glucose, EUC and troponin (action_type=investigation, status=planned, responsible_person=doctor)

bad.reason: Doctor recommends Cartia daily, one tablet in the morning; 'every morning' is not stated.
bad.text: Take Cartia one tablet every morning (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: Chest pain with exertional breathlessness was specifically asked about and initially denied: patient said 'No. No chest pain. I wouldn't call it pain.'
Exertional chest tightness was described as 'like a band across my chest'.
Patient reported no arm pain/radiation: 'No pain in the jaw' was recorded, but the doctor also warned about pain going into the arm and the patient did not report arm pain.
Negative finding not recorded: patient said 'I don't think I've been dizzy' in response to red-flag questioning about dizziness with symptoms.
Negative finding not recorded: patient denied asthma when asked 'Any diabetes, asthma, operations?'

Aspirin/Cartia instruction is recorded wrongly: doctor said 'take the Cartia every day from now, one tablet in the morning', not 'every morning' specifically as a current medication frequency; this was a new instruction changing prior inconsistent use.
GTN plan missing qualifier: doctor said to use the GTN spray under the tongue if tightness comes on and doesn't ease when he rests.
Follow-up plan detail missing: doctor said to come back in a week for the results 'regardless'.
Results communication plan missing: if something urgent is found, the clinic will contact the patient; otherwise do not wait by the phone and review at the one-week appointment.
